policy_title: Invest in home insulation, green heating, and climate adaptation for homes
stated: Invest £29bn over five years to insulate homes to EPC B standard or above, £9bn for non-fossil fuel heating systems like heat pumps, and £7bn to adapt homes for hotter summers, prioritising a local authority-led retrofit programme.

source.quote: Elected Greens will invest: • £29bn over the next five years to insulate homes to EPC B standard or above, as part of a ten-year programme. £12bn of this will be to retrofit the social housing stock and £17bn as grants to retrofit privately owned homes to a similar standard. • £9bn over the next five years for heating systems (e.g. heat pumps) for homes and other buildings. • £7bn over the next five years to adapt homes to avoid over-heating in the hotter summers.

bearing_set.reason: Insulating homes to EPC B and replacing fossil-fuel heating directly reduces household energy bills, a core cost-of-living indicator.
Switching from gas boilers to heat pumps and improving insulation directly cuts domestic carbon emissions, a primary driver of the UK's emissions trajectory.

Cold, under-insulated homes drive cold-related morbidity, excess winter deaths, and respiratory/cardiovascular NHS demand; at the scale of a £29bn retrofit programme this is a well-documented pathway that would materially reduce that health burden.

A £29bn + £9bn + £7bn = ~£45bn spending commitment over five years is a material fiscal obligation; whether it improves or worsens the debt path depends on funding mechanism and long-run savings (reduced NHS cold-related costs, lower energy imports), but the scale alone demands an O12 verdict.

Lower-income households typically live in the worst-insulated homes and spend the highest share of income on energy; a local authority-led programme skews savings disproportionately toward this group, creating a compressible distributional effect on income inequality.

membership_note: Five genuine bearings: the policy's primary purpose hits O6 (decarbonisation) and O2 (lower energy bills); O3 follows the well-evidenced cold-homes-to-health pathway; O12 captures the material fiscal commitment; and O14 reflects the documented pro-poor distributional skew of retrofit gains. O1 (housing affordability/supply) and O13 (aggregate growth) are secondary or too diffuse to clear the non-negligible bar independently.
